title: The Sun
bodyParagraphs: One of the seven classical planets. Called Helios by the Greeks, adopted by the Romans as Sol, our Sun comes from the old Saxon Sunna. The sun is both a glorious crown and an all seeing eye in the sky. Besides naming the first day of the week, we define a year by the position of the sun in the sky from one winter solstice to the next.
The diameter of the Planetarium dome defines the scale of the model. At 82’ 10” dome is 55 million times smaller than the sun.

title: Mercury
bodyParagraphs: One of the seven classical planets. Called Apollo in the morning and Hermes in the evening by the Greeks, they soon realized it was the same planet. Adopted by the Romans as Mercury, the messenger god, we honor him in the middle of the week. The Latin ‘dies Mercurii’ became ‘el miércoles’ in Spanish. The Old English Wōdnesdæg, honoring the god of the dead, became Wednesday in modern English.
At the model scale of 55 million to one, Mercury is about 3.5” (88mm) in diameter and 2/3 mile (1 km) from the planetarium dome.

title: Venus
bodyParagraphs: One of the seven classical planets. Called Aphrodite by the Greeks, she represents love and fertility. Adopted by the Romans as Venus, we honor her at the end of the work week. The Latin dies Veneris became el Viernes in Spanish. The Old English Frīgedæg meaning the day of the Anglo-Saxon goddess Frīg, goddess of motherhood, became Friday in modern English.
At the model scale of 55 million to one, Venus is about 8.7” (217mm) in diameter and 1 1/4 mile (2 km) from the planetarium dome.

title: Earth
bodyParagraphs: Not one of the seven classical planets, Earth was the center of the ancient Universe. Ancients thought of earth as a mother goddess that is also the primary fertility deity. Copernicus proposed we are not the center of the universe during the renaissance. Galileo provided visual evidence. Kepler did the math. The Apollo astronauts showed us its unique beauty from afar.
At the model scale of 55 million to one, Earth is a soccer (fútbol) ball over 1.6 miles (2.5 km) from the dome, the moon is a baseball 23 feet from the earth.

title: Mars
bodyParagraphs: One of the seven classical planets. Mars is the god of war and farmers. Soldiering season starts with planting and ends with harvest. Mardi is third day in Latin, the Norse god Tiw is equivalent of Mars which gives Tuesday.
At the model scale of 55 million to one, Mars is about 5” (123mm) in diameter and 2 1/2 miles (4 km) from the planetarium dome.

title: Ceres
bodyParagraphs: Ceres, named after the Roman goddess of agriculture, is a dwarf planet in the main asteroid belt between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter. It was the first known asteroid, discovered on 1 January 1801 by Giuseppe Piazzi at Palermo Astronomical Observatory in Sicily, and announced as a new planet. Ceres was later classified as an asteroid and more recently as a dwarf planet, the only one not beyond the orbit of Neptune and the largest that does not have a moon.
At the model scale of 55 million to one, Ceres is a small sphere at 5/8” (16mm) in diameter and 5 miles (8 km) from the planetarium dome.

title: Asteroids (Vesta)
bodyParagraphs: Vesta, the virgin goddess of home and hearth, was discovered by the German astronomer Heinrich Wilhelm Matthias Olbers on 29 March 1807.
At the model scale of 55 million to one, Vesta is the largest asteroid at 3/8” (10mm) in diameter and 5 miles (8 km) from the planetarium dome.

title: Jupiter
bodyParagraphs: One of the seven classical planets. Jupiter is the god of the sky and thunder and king of the Gods. We honor him on the 5th day of the week in Spanish as jueves. Thor, the Norse god of thunder gives us Thursday.
At the model scale of 55 million to one, Jupiter is the largest sphere at 100” (2.5m) in diameter and 9 miles (14 km) from the planetarium dome.

title: Saturn
bodyParagraphs: One of the seven classical planets. Saturn is god of time. He is adopted from the Greek Titan Cronus. The Romans named Saturday for the god Saturn. His planet, Saturn, controlled the first hour of that day. Saturn's consort was his sister Ops, with whom he fathered Jupiter, Neptune, Pluto, Juno, Ceres and Vesta.

At the model scale of 55 million to one, Saturn’s rings are the largest element of the Los Angeles model 16’ (5m) across. The sphere is 7’ (2.1m) in diameter and 16 miles (26 km) from the planetarium dome.

title: Uranus
bodyParagraphs: Uranus is the Greek god of the sky and heavens. He is son and husband of the goddess of the earth and worlds, Gaia. Uranus was likely observed in antiquity, most notably by Greek astronomer Hipparchus in 128 BCE, who likely cataloged it as a faint, fixed star. William Herschel is credited with the official discovery in 1781.
At the model scale of 55 million to one, Uranus is 36” (91cm) in diameter and 32 miles (51 km) from the planetarium dome.

title: Neptune
bodyParagraphs: Neptune is the god of water and the sea. Galileo was the first person to see Neptune in 1612. He is not credited with the discovery. He thought Neptune was a "fixed star" instead of a planet. In 1846, Urbain Le Verrier made calculations for the location of a new planet based on disturbances in the orbit of Uranus. Le Verrier sent a letter and urged Berlin Observatory astronomer Johann Gottfried Galle to search with the observatory's refractor. On the evening of 23 September 1846, the day Galle received the letter, he discovered Neptune. It was found 1° from where Le Verrier had thought it would be. Neptune became the first planet to be discovered by mathematical calculations instead of a telescope.
At the model scale of 55 million to one, Neptune is 35” (89cm) in diameter and 51 miles (82 km) from the planetarium dome.

title: Pluto
bodyParagraphs: Pluto is the ruler of the underworld. Pluto is a dwarf planet in the Kuiper belt, a ring of bodies beyond the orbit of Neptune. Pluto was discovered in 1930 by Clyde W. Tombaugh at Lowell Observatory in Flagstaff, Arizona.

At the model scale of 55 million to one, Pluto is 1 3/4” (45mm) in diameter. Its moon Charon is 7/8” (22mm) 14” (357mm) away. Having a highly elliptical orbit, it could be 50 to 83 miles (80 to 133 km) from the planetarium dome.

title: Sedna
bodyParagraphs: Sedna is the goddess of the sea and marine animals. Sedna was discovered by Michael Brown, Chad Trujillo, and David Rabinowitz in 2003 at Palomar Observatory near San Diego, California.
At the model scale of 55 million to one, Sedna is 5/8” (16mm) in diameter. She could be 1500 miles (2400km) from the planetarium dome. The most distant object in the model.
